en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 58: The Discourse to Prince Abhaya (Abhayarājakumārasutta)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then Prince Abhaya approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta;
having approached, he paid homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and sat down to one side. As Prince Abhaya was sitting there to one side, [the Nigaṇṭha spoke].
The Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta said this:
“Come, prince, refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.
In this way, a fine report of your reputation will spread abroad:”
“Prince Abhaya has brought a challenge to the ascetic Gotama, who possesses such great psychic power and such great majesty.
“But how, venerable sir, shall I bring a challenge to the ascetic Gotama, who possesses such great psychic power and such great majesty?
“Come, prince, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, speak thus to the ascetic Gotama:”
“Would the Tathāgata, Bhante, speak that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others?
If the ascetic Gotama, when asked thus, answers:
“The Tathāgata, Prince, would speak that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others,” then you should say this to him:
‘But then, venerable sir, what is the distinction between you and an ordinary person?
For even an ordinary person might speak that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others.
And if the ascetic Gotama, being thus questioned, answers thus:
“Prince, the Tathāgata would not utter such speech as is unpleasant and disagreeable to others. To him you should say:
“But then, venerable sir, why was it declared of Devadatta:
‘Devadatta is destined for the states of deprivation, Devadatta is destined for hell, Devadatta will remain there for an eon, Devadatta is incurable’?”
"And because of those words, Devadatta became angry and displeased.
Prince, when the ascetic Gotama is asked this twofold question by you, he will be unable either to spit it out or to swallow it down.
It would be just like a man with an iron ball stuck in his throat, who would be unable both to spit it out and unable to swallow it down.
"In the same way, Prince, when the ascetic Gotama is asked this twofold question, he will be unable either to swallow it up or to spit it out.
"So be it, venerable sir," Prince Abhaya replied to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta.
Having assented, he rose from his seat, paid homage to Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, and keeping him to his right, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As Prince Abhaya was sitting there, he looked up at the sun and thought:
"It is not the right time today to challenge the Blessed One to a debate."
"Today, in my own residence, I shall refute the Blessed One's doctrine," he said, and addressed the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal, together with three others.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Prince Abhaya, having understood the Blessed One’s acceptance, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and outer robe, went to the residence of Prince Abhaya. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then Prince Abhaya, with his own hands, served and satisfied the Blessed One with excellent hard and soft foods.
Then Prince Abhaya, when the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, Prince Abhaya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, would the Tathāgata speak that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others?”
“In this matter, prince, it is not one-sided.
“Venerable sir, in this matter the Nigaṇṭhas have perished.
“But why, prince, do you say this?”
“‘In this matter, Bhante, the Nigaṇṭhas have been defeated.
[The Blessed One said: “In this case, Bhante, I approached the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta;
having approached, I paid homage to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and sat down to one side. While I was sitting there to one side, Bhante, the Nigaṇṭha...”
Nāṭaputta said this:
“Come, prince, refute the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama.
In this way, a fine reputation will spread about you:”
‘The prince Abhaya has brought a charge against the ascetic Gotama, who is so powerful and so majestic!
When this was said, venerable sir, I said to the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta:
‘But how, venerable sir, shall I bring a charge against the ascetic Gotama, who is so powerful and so majestic?’”
"Come, prince, go to where the ascetic Gotama is; having approached him, say this to the ascetic Gotama:
'Venerable sir, would the Tathāgata speak such speech as that which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others?
If, when asked thus, the ascetic Gotama answers you in this way:"
“Prince, if the Tathāgata were to speak that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others,” you should say this to him:
“In that case, venerable sir, what is the distinction between you and an ordinary person?
For even an ordinary person might speak that speech which is unpleasant and disagreeable to others.”
But if, when asked thus, the ascetic Gotama should answer:
“Prince, the Tathāgata would not utter such speech as is unpleasant and disagreeable to others,” then you should say to him:
“In that case, venerable sir, why was Devadatta declared [by you] to be...?”
“Is Devadatta bound for the states of misery? Is Devadatta bound for hell? Is Devadatta destined to remain there for an eon? Is Devadatta incurable?
And because of those words, Devadatta became angry and displeased.
Prince, when the ascetic Gotama is asked this double-edged question by you, he will be unable either to spit it out or to swallow it down.
"Just as if an iron hook were stuck in a man's throat, such that he could neither spit it out nor swallow it, even so, Prince,
when the ascetic Gotama is asked this double-pronged question, he will be unable to spit it out and unable to swallow it.
At that time, a young, weak infant was sitting on the lap of Prince Abhaya.
Then the Blessed One said this to Prince Abhaya:
“What do you think, prince?
If this boy, through your negligence or through the negligence of his nurse, were to put a stick or a pebble into his mouth, what would you do to him?”
“I would fetch it, Bhante.
If, Bhante, I were unable to fetch it at once, I would grasp its head with my left hand, curve my right index finger, and fetch it even if it were bleeding. Why is that?
Because, Bhante, this body of mine is so dear to me.”
“Venerable sir, I have compassion for the prince.

“In the same way, prince, whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and which is also unpleasant and disagreeable to others—that speech the Tathāgata does not utter.
And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true and correct, yet unbeneficial, and which is also unpleasant and disagreeable to others—that speech too the Tathāgata does not utter.”
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata knows a speech that is true, real, and beneficial, yet is unpleasant and disagreeable to others, the Tathāgata knows the proper time for the delivery of such speech.
When the Tathāgata knows a speech that is untrue, unreal, and not beneficial, even if it is pleasant and agreeable to others, the Tathāgata does not utter that speech.
And when the Tathāgata knows a speech that is true, real, but not beneficial, even if it is pleasant and agreeable to others, the Tathāgata likewise does not utter that speech.

And whatever speech the Tathāgata knows to be true, real, and beneficial, and which is pleasing and agreeable to others—in that case, the Tathāgata is one who knows the proper time for the explanation of such speech.
For what reason?
Because, Prince, the Tathāgata has compassion for living beings.”
“Venerable sir, when wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, wise householders, and wise ascetics formulate a question and approach the Tathāgata to ask it,
does the Blessed One first reflect in his mind, ‘Those who approach me and ask such a question,
I shall answer them thus when asked,’ or does this occur to the Tathāgata spontaneously at that very moment?”
“In that case, prince, I shall question you about this very matter; answer it as you see fit.
What do you think, prince:
are you skilled in the parts and components of a chariot?”
“In this way, venerable sir, I am skilled in the parts and components of a chariot.
“What do you think, prince?
Suppose people were to approach you and ask:”
“‘What are these various parts of the chariot?

Would you have previously reflected in your mind, ‘When they approach me and ask me this, being thus questioned, I shall answer them thus,’ or would this simply occur to you spontaneously on the spot?
“I am, venerable sir, a well-known charioteer, skilled in the various parts of a chariot.”
“All the parts and members of my chariot are well known to me.
It occurs to me that I could explain this by its very position.
“In the same way, Prince, those wise khattiyas, wise brahmins, and wise householders—”
Even when learned ascetics, having prepared a question, approach the Tathāgata and ask it,
this occurs to the Tathāgata spontaneously.
For what reason?

“Because, Prince, the Tathāgata has thoroughly penetrated the element of phenomena (dhammadhātu), and because he has thoroughly penetrated that element of phenomena, this occurs to the Tathāgata spontaneously.
When this was said, Prince Abhaya said to the Blessed One:
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! … [as before] …”
“From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, I go for refuge.
The eighth discourse, the *Abhayarājakumāra Sutta*, is finished.
